issues.legal_issue: A municipal corporation may seal premises that are being used commercially contrary to their authorized residential use.
material_facts: Residential premises were being converted to commercial use without authorization.
The statutory definition of erecting a building included specified conversions of a building's use, including conversion to a shop or other trade premises.
The municipal law prohibited changing the use of land or a building without written permission and authorized sealing in connection with enforcement of its building-control provisions.
issues.conclusion: The municipal commissioner has power to seal premises that are being misused, even if no demolition or stoppage order has first been made.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 331, 336, 343, 344, 345A and 347 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, read together, conversion of a building's use can fall within the statutory concept of erecting a building, and Section 345A permits sealing before or after a demolition or stoppage order. The relevant definitions of conversion and erecting a building in Bye-Laws 2.17 and 2.85 support this interpretation. The Act's planning and use restrictions are binding, and no right exists to use a building contrary to its authorized purpose.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_municipal_sealing: The proceeding concerns whether a municipal authority may seal premises because of their use.
predicates.residential_premises_used_for_trade: A person uses premises authorized for residential purposes to carry on a trade or commercial activity.
predicates.use_not_authorized: The commercial use has not been authorized by the applicable planning or municipal authority.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns sealing and unauthorized trade is carried on in residential premises, the municipality may seal the misused premises.

issues.legal_issue: A development authority cannot use its power to seal unauthorized development to seal premises solely because their use has changed contrary to the permitted use.
material_facts: The sealing power at issue applied to unauthorized development that could be removed or discontinued under the development law.
The disputed conduct was misuse of premises, and the development law did not treat misuse as development for purposes of that sealing power.
The statutory scheme transferred responsibility for developed areas to the relevant local authority when that authority assumed responsibility for their amenities.
issues.conclusion: The development authority has no power under the Delhi Development Act to seal premises on account of misuse alone.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d) of the Delhi Development Act defines development by reference to building, engineering, mining or other operations, material change in a building or land, and redevelopment. Sections 30 and 31 address removal or discontinuance of development, while Section 31A permits sealing of such development. Sections 12, 22A and 36 describe the development-area scheme and the transfer of responsibility to a local authority. The words such development in Section 31A do not extend its sealing power to misuse that is not development.

predicates.proceeding_concerns_development_authorit: The proceeding concerns whether a development authority may seal premises because of their use.
predicates.premises_used_against_permitted_purpose: A person uses premises for a purpose different from the purpose permitted for them.
predicates.conduct_is_only_change_of_use: The conduct at issue is a change in use alone, rather than unauthorized development within the statutory meaning.

issues.definition: When a development authority's sealing power is invoked for premises used contrary to their permitted purpose and the conduct is only a change of use, the authority cannot seal them for that misuse.

issues.legal_issue: Large-scale unauthorized commercial use of residential premises requires prompt, phased enforcement rather than further delay for a general survey.
material_facts: Commercial use of residential premises had continued on a large scale despite repeated orders and years of inaction by the authorities.
The authority had identified roads with major violations, including roads where commercial use affected more than half of the buildings.
The court found that further delay for a proposed survey would postpone enforcement and that the identified major violations allowed action to begin.
issues.conclusion: The municipal authority must begin time-bound enforcement against major violations, starting with affected roads at least 80 feet wide; it must publicize the violations, allow a period for voluntary compliance, and then seal premises where the misuse continues. The court also directed disconnection of electricity and water after that compliance period and required reporting and assistance in the sealing process.
issues.legal_principle: The rule of law requires enforcement of planning and municipal laws, and public authorities have constitutional duties to protect citizens' rights and the environment. Mass non-enforcement cannot justify indefinite delay; where the violations are identifiable, enforcement may proceed in phases, beginning with major violations. The court relied on its earlier enforcement orders, including M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2004) 6 SCC 588, and referred to Ahuja Property Developers (P) Ltd. v. M.C.D., DDA v. Rajinder Mittal, ANZ Grindlays Bank v. Commissioner, M.C.D., and Anil Kumar Khurana v. M.C.D.

rule.if: public_interest_enforcement_proceeding and large_scale_residential_commercial_misuse and authorities_failed_to_enforce_law and major_violations_identifiable

predicates.public_interest_enforcement_proceeding: The proceeding seeks enforcement of land-use laws for the protection of residents and the public.
predicates.large_scale_residential_commercial_misus: Many residential premises are being used commercially contrary to their authorized use.
predicates.authorities_failed_to_enforce_law: The responsible authorities have failed to stop the unlawful use despite prior complaints or directions.
predicates.major_violations_identifiable: The locations or categories of major violations can be identified without awaiting a general survey.

issues.definition: When widespread misuse has gone unenforced in a public-interest proceeding and major violations are identifiable, the municipality must begin time-bound enforcement by sealing premises where the misuse continues.

issues.legal_issue: An ad hoc registration scheme cannot be applied to regularize large-scale commercial misuse that conflicts with the planned use of residential premises.
material_facts: A municipal scheme proposed ad hoc registration of commercial establishments in certain nonconforming or residential areas.
The scheme did not apply to the planned colonies and housing schemes relevant to the large-scale misuse under consideration.
The court had stayed the scheme and found that applying it to the misuse at issue would regularize illegalities and encourage further violations.
issues.conclusion: The ad hoc registration scheme has no applicability to the large-scale misuse under consideration and cannot be used to regularize it.
issues.legal_principle: Land-use restrictions in approved plans and municipal laws are binding. An administrative registration scheme cannot be used to validate commercial use that those restrictions prohibit; a scheme that would regularize such illegality and encourage further violations cannot govern the misuse before the court.

predicates.proceeding_considers_regularization_sche: The proceeding considers whether an administrative scheme can register commercial use of premises.
predicates.scheme_covers_commercial_use_in_nonconfo: The scheme offers registration for commercial establishments in areas where that use may not conform to the planned land use.
predicates.proposed_use_conflicts_with_binding_land: The commercial use conflicts with the binding plan governing the premises.

issues.definition: When a registration scheme covers nonconforming commercial use that conflicts with the binding land-use plan, the scheme cannot regularize that misuse.
